ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that impair functioning. Diagnosis relies on DSM‑5 criteria, clinical history, and rule‑out of other causes. Management combines behavioral strategies and medication, tailored to severity and comorbidities.

sections.p: ADHD is defined by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity‑impulsivity that interfere with functioning. DSM‑5 requires symptoms before age 12, present in two settings, and not better explained by another disorder.
b: Symptoms must be present for >6 months
Impact on social, academic, or occupational domains

sections.p: Severity is graded as mild, moderate, or severe based on number of symptoms, functional impairment, and comorbidities. The Vanderbilt or Conners scales help quantify severity.

ADHD is multifactorial: strong genetic component, neurobiological differences in dopamine pathways, prenatal exposures, and early childhood adversity. In low‑resource settings, infections (HIV, malaria) and nutritional deficiencies can exacerbate symptoms.

Children show distractibility, fidgeting, and difficulty following instructions. Adults may report restlessness, poor time management, and relationship problems. Symptoms vary by subtype: inattentive, hyperactive‑impulsive, or combined.
Investigations aim to exclude other causes and assess comorbidities. No single test confirms ADHD.

t.b: Low IQ suggests comorbid learning disorder
Abnormal results warrant treatment of sleep disorder

sections.p: Severe impulsivity can lead to accidents, self‑harm, or substance misuse. Untreated ADHD increases risk of academic failure, unemployment, and psychiatric comorbidity.

Treat the underlying cause first, then use behavioral therapy and medication. Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) are first‑line; non‑stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are alternatives. Monitor for growth suppression, hypertension, and psychiatric side effects.
b: Behavioral therapy: parent training, classroom interventions

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, growth, blood pressure, and medication tolerance is essential. Early intervention reduces long‑term disability.
ADHD can mimic learning disorders, anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, thyroid disease, and lead poisoning.
b: Learning disability: poor academic performance but intact attention

sections.p: Normal IQ does not exclude ADHD; low blood pressure can mask stimulant side effects; normal thyroid tests may miss subclinical hypothyroidism.
